Fossil fuels and climate finance among deep divisions that have pushed UN summit beyond its official end

Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty ImagesAjit Niranjan (now), Matthew Pearce (earlier)Fri 20 Nov 2026 18.11 GMTFirst published on Fri 20 Nov 2026 07.10 GMTShareFrom 20m ago17.50 GMTChina appears to have endorsed the flagship 35x35 electrification pledge, as momentum gathers behind at least of the key goals of this summit.

In a joint statement with Australia, published by the state-run Xinhua news agency, the two countries said they welcome “growing international ambition and cooperation on electrification to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 on a voluntary basis.”

The announcement, spotted by Carbon Brief, also commits China and Australia to keeping the 1.5C goal “within reach” and minimise the magnitude and duration of any overshoot. In keeping with an emerging theme of the summit, though, it does not mention fossil fuels.

Here are the highlights from the 12th day of the 31st UN climate summit, which has now run into overtime:

African negotiators accused rich countries of undermining the credibility of Cop by failing to provide needed cash

Civil society activists called Antalya 2026 the ‘worst Cop ever’

Small island states said overshoot of 1.5C was the ‘unacceptable’ result of advancing profit over people

France led a multi-country push to get the ‘transition away from fossil fuels’ back into the deal

China appeared to endorse the Cop Presidency’s flagship electrification pledge

Thanks for following – we’ll be back tomorrow morning for what may (or may not!) prove to be the final day of the contentious summit. We look forward to guiding you through it.

20m ago17.50 GMTChina appears to have endorsed the flagship 35x35 electrification pledge, as momentum gathers behind at least of the key goals of this summit.

30m ago17.40 GMTGraham ReadfearnMy colleague Gabrielle Canon and I have been speaking to people at Cop31 about carbon capture technology.

Saudi Arabia is understood to be among the countries pushing for Carbon Capture Utilization and Storage (CCUS) to be strongly referenced in a final agreement being negotiated by more than 190 countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey.

As the talks reached their final hours, the term “fossil fuels” was removed from a draft of the agreement, while CCUS was referenced as a way to help the planet to minimise overshooting the 1.5C temperature goal agreed in Paris.

Neil Grant, a senior expert on mitigation at advisory group Climate Analytics, said CCUS was being put into the text “because the fossil fuel interests want it in there.”

“It’s a Trojan horse for fossil fuel interests,” he said.

The text contains references to “working towards” 2.5 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide being captured and stored per year by 2035, although these figures are in brackets meaning they are references that are being negotiated for inclusion.

Grant said CCUS projects around the world could only currently capture about 60m tonnes of CO2 if they all worked to capacity, but he said the reality was they were only working at about half of that.

“To scale to 2.5 gigatonnes would require a 40 fold increase over a decade for incredibly complex technologies. About 80% of all large-scale CCS projects have been delayed or cancelled,” he said.

For context, 60 Mt of CO2 is less than 0.2% of the 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 emitted from burning fossil fuels in 2026, according to the Global Carbon Budget.

Carbon capture is a small but significant component of scientific roadmaps to the stop the planet heating, particularly in heavy industries that lack clean alternatives. But today, CCUS is most often deployed by oil and gas companies to capture CO2 during fossil fuel extraction. It is distinct from Carbon Dioxide Removal – a set of technologies including direct air capture that tries to gather CO2 from the atmosphere and lock it away.

Dr Peter Schniering, founder and CEO of the Germany-based thinktank Future Cleantech Architects, said the business case for CCUS “remains weak”.

He said: “Capturing CO2 requires additional energy, while transport and storage add substantial costs. This means all projects would ultimately depend on government subsidies or high carbon prices to become economically viable.”

Both technologies have had a strong presence in Antalya, with a dedicated CDR pavilion and CCUS being showcased at country pavilions, including Saudi Arabia’s.

“CDR still sounds unreal to people but we spent a whole year trying to make it into the agenda of Cop31,” Göker Avci, a decarbonization strategist at CDR Türkiye told the Guardian last week.

“We spoke with the presidency about making it into the final decision and they have started to realise the potential.”

While both the International Energy Agency and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change have said pulling the world back from overshooting the 1.5C temperature goal will need the help of carbon dioxide removal technologies, so far, promises have come up short.

“There’s a lot of uncertainties surrounding these techniques including their climate effectiveness but also their impacts on nature and people,” John Verdieck, the Director of International Climate Policy at The Nature Conservancy told the Guardian.

The 44 Least Developed Countries have asked for CCUS to be removed from the final text and a fossil fuel phaseout to be reinserted.

2h ago16.36 GMTJoe Pinner‘Too often, finance moves slower than floods’

Every day for the two weeks of Cop31 I’ve been speaking to young climate activists. Today I spoke to Sidra Riaz, 29, from Pakistan.

In 2022, she founded Environmental Change Makers, a youth-led climate education initiative, during the devastating Pakistan floods of 2022.

View image in fullscreenSidra Riaz speaks at a Sustainable Development Policy Institute seminar on climate anxiety and its impact on women, in Islamabad, Pakistan. Photograph: UN Women“In 2022, floods reached my village in Punjab. Water swallowed fields, homes and the roads children used to walk to school. I come from a community that did almost nothing to cause this crisis, yet we pay for it first.

“That year I started Environmental Change Makers. We have since brought climate education to 1,200 children, many of them in flood-hit areas like Sindh and Balochistan. When I think about my future, I feel two things at once. I feel fear, because every monsoon now arrives as a threat. I also feel resolve, because I have seen what communities can do when someone backs them.

“I am at Cop31 to carry those voices into the rooms where decisions get made. So far, I have seen real energy in the pavilions, but the negotiating rooms still circle around who pays and how much. Too often, finance moves slower than floods. If I could change one thing, I would give frontline communities, especially women and young people, a real seat at the negotiating table – not just a pavilion.

“From this Cop, I want adaptation finance that reaches villages like mine. I want a loss and damage fund that pays out fast. And I want women and girls at the centre of resilience, because they hold their communities together when disaster hits.”

2h ago16.22 GMTGraham ReadfearnWe do now have a bit more clarity on what’s happening here.

The closing plenary is going to start at 8pm Antalya time, but this is just to close off items that have been negotiated already.

Countries may or may not get a new draft text to mull over tonight, but this is going to go to Saturday.

The plenary should also outline more clearly what’s going to happen next.

2h ago16.08 GMTGraham ReadfearnThere’s been a noticeable shift in the energy among journalists here in the media centre at Cop31 since it became clear we were not going to finish on time.

This should be a shock to nobody.
